subject: Polity
description: National Human Rights Commission, National Commission for Women, statutory basis, composition

questions.stem: The NATIONAL HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION (NHRC) of India was established in:

options.option_text: 1950, alongside the framing of the Indian Constitution
1993, under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
2005, alongside the Right to Information Act, 2005
1976, soon after the Emergency-era civil-rights crackdown

questions.explanation: NHRC established by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (PHR Act). Inaugurated on 12 October 1993; HQ at New Delhi. STATUTORY (not constitutional) body. Mandate: investigate human rights violations by public officials, intervene in court proceedings, study international treaties, promote awareness. Powers: civil court for evidence-gathering; recommendations are not binding but carry moral weight. India became a signatory to the Paris Principles (1991) on national human rights institutions, which prompted setting up NHRC.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Who can be appointed as the CHAIRPERSON of the NHRC?

options.option_text: Any retired senior IAS officer of the Government of India
A retired Chief Justice of India or Supreme Court judge
The current Vice-President of India during his fixed tenure
The senior-most member of the ruling party in Parliament

questions.explanation: NHRC Chairperson — earlier required to be a RETIRED CJI; the 2019 amendment expanded eligibility to retired CJI OR retired Supreme Court Judge. Other members: 1 retired SC judge, 1 retired HC chief justice, 3 persons (incl. one woman) with knowledge of human rights. Plus ex-officio: chairs of National Commissions for SCs/STs/OBCs/Women/Minorities/Children, Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. Tenure: 3 years or until age 70 (post-2019 amendment, raised from 5 yrs and 70 was always the cap). Appointed by President on the recommendation of a 6-member committee headed by PM.

questions.stem: The NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW) was established under:

options.option_text: Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India
National Commission for Women Act, 1990
Domestic Violence Act enacted in the year 2005
Right to Information Act of the year 2005

questions.explanation: NCW — created by the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. Began functioning January 1992. Headquarters: New Delhi. Statutory body (not constitutional). Functions: investigate constitutional + legal safeguards for women, recommend remedial action, take up complaints, fund research, review existing laws. Composition: Chairperson + 5 members (each with relevant experience), all appointed by Centre. Article 15(3) PERMITS special provisions for women + children but is not the legal basis for NCW. The Domestic Violence Act 2005 is enforced by Protection Officers + magistrates, not by NCW itself.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The recommendations of the NHRC are:

options.option_text: Legally binding on the Centre and on every state government
Non-binding but generally acted upon as moral persuasion
Equivalent to a Supreme Court order in every legal sense
Binding only on Union Territories under direct Centre rule

questions.explanation: NHRC recommendations are NOT legally binding — only persuasive. Government must respond within 1 month explaining if it accepts or rejects. NHRC can move the courts (via Section 18 of the Act) and approach the Supreme Court / High Courts directly for enforcement of human rights. Critics call NHRC a 'toothless tiger' for this reason. Distractor 3 — only the SC's own orders are binding. Distractor 4 — UT vs state distinction doesn't change the binding nature.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT among the major functions of the NCW?

options.option_text: Investigating and reporting on women's safeguards under law
Issuing legally binding rulings against the perpetrators
Looking into individual complaints of women's rights violations
Recommending amendments to laws for better gender protection

questions.explanation: NCW does NOT issue legally binding rulings against perpetrators (it can only investigate, recommend, refer to police/courts). Distractor 1 = real function. Distractor 3 = real function (NCW receives complaints, especially via its Complaint and Counselling Cell). Distractor 4 = real function (e.g., NCW's recommendations led to changes in dowry, sexual-harassment laws). The Commission also reports annually to Parliament.

questions.stem: STATE HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSIONS (SHRCs) — separate from NHRC — were also provided for under the 1993 Act. SHRC chairperson must be:

options.option_text: A retired Indian Civil Service officer of cabinet rank
A retired chief justice or judge of a High Court
Senior member of the state's ruling political party only
Director general of police of the concerned state

questions.explanation: SHRC Chairperson — retired Chief Justice of HC or Judge of HC (eligibility expanded by 2019 Amendment). Members: judicial member + 1 person with HR knowledge. SHRCs handle violations under STATE LIST + CONCURRENT LIST subjects; NHRC handles UNION LIST (and concurrent issues that the state has not addressed). NHRC can transfer cases to SHRC; SHRC can refer matters to NHRC. As of 2024, ~26 states have established SHRCs.

questions.stem: Of the following women, who was the FIRST chairperson of the National Commission for Women (NCW)?

options.option_text: Lalitha Kumaramangalam, who served from 2014 to 2017
Jayanti Patnaik, the first chairperson from 1992 to 1995
Dr Vibha Parthasarathi, who served from 1999 to 2002
Mamta Sharma, who served from 2011 to 2014 in the role

questions.explanation: Jayanti Patnaik — FIRST chairperson of NCW (1992-95). Mother of Naveen Patnaik (former CM, Odisha). She was also a former MP. Subsequent chairpersons: V. Mohini Giri (1995-98), Vibha Parthasarathi (1999-2002), Poornima Advani (2002-05), Girija Vyas (2005-11), Mamta Sharma (2011-14), Lalitha Kumaramangalam (2014-17), Rekha Sharma (2018-24), Vijaya Rahatkar (2024-).
